content: Psychological therapies designed for parents of children and adolescents with chronic illnesses aim to enhance parenting behaviors, improve parental mental health, and positively impact child and family functioning. These therapies have been evaluated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to determine their efficacy and potential adverse effects. The updated review includes 44 RCTs with a total of 4697 participants. The studies involved children with various chronic conditions, including asthma, cancer, chronic pain, diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, skin diseases, and traumatic brain injury. The psychological interventions assessed included cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), family therapy, motivational interviewing, multisystemic therapy, and problem-solving therapy (PST). The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations due to heterogeneity, imprecision, and publication bias. Parenting Behavior Outcomes by Medical Condition: Psychological therapies may improve parenting behaviors, such as reducing maladaptive or overly solicitous behaviors, in parents of children with cancer, chronic pain, diabetes, and traumatic brain injury. For parents of children with cancer, improvements were observed both post-treatment (SMD −0.28) and at follow-up (SMD −0.21), based on low-quality evidence. For parents of children with chronic pain, improvements were noted post-treatment (SMD −0.29) and at follow-up (SMD −0.35), supported by moderate-quality evidence. For parents of children with diabetes, improvements were seen post-treatment (SMD −1.39), but the evidence was of very low quality. For parents of children with traumatic brain injury, improvements were observed post-treatment (SMD −0.74), also based on very low-quality evidence. Data were insufficient to evaluate the effects of psychological therapies on parenting behaviors for other medical conditions. Parent Mental Health Outcomes by Medical Condition: Psychological therapies may improve parental mental health, such as reducing symptoms of depression and anxiety, in parents of children with cancer and chronic pain. For parents of children with cancer, improvements were observed post-treatment (SMD −0.21) and at follow-up (SMD −0.23), with evidence quality ranging from high to moderate. For parents of children with chronic pain, improvements were noted post-treatment (SMD −0.24) and at follow-up (SMD −0.20), based on low-quality evidence. No significant improvements in parental mental health were observed for parents of children with diabetes post-treatment (SMD −0.24), with very low-quality evidence. Data were insufficient to evaluate the effects of psychological therapies on parental mental health for other medical conditions. Parenting Behavior Outcomes by Therapy Type: CBT may improve parenting behaviors post-treatment (SMD −0.45) and at follow-up (SMD −0.26), based on lowto moderate-quality evidence. PST may also improve parenting behaviors post-treatment (SMD −0.39) and at follow-up (SMD −0.54), but the evidence quality was low to very low. Parent Mental Health Outcomes by Therapy Type: PST may improve parental mental health post-treatment (SMD −0.30) and at follow-up (SMD −0.21), supported by moderate-quality evidence. CBT did not show significant improvements in parental mental health post-treatment (SMD −0.19) or at follow-up (SMD −0.07), with very low-quality evidence. Adverse Events: Most studies (32) did not report on adverse events. In six studies, no adverse events were reported, and in another six studies, adverse events were noted but were not attributed to psychological therapy. The quality of evidence for adverse events was rated as moderate. Conclusions: Psychological therapies, particularly CBT and PST, may improve parenting behaviors in parents of children with chronic illnesses such as cancer, chronic pain, diabetes, and traumatic brain injury. PST may also improve parental mental health, particularly for parents of children with cancer and chronic pain. However, the overall quality of evidence is low, and data are insufficient to evaluate many outcomes. Further research is needed to strengthen the evidence base and assess the safety and efficacy of these interventions comprehensively.
